opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because there's a real tension there. On one hand, to get peak performance you really have to write code that's quite specific to the hardware. With FlashAttention, each generation we've had to rethink things. On Ampere it was about tiling and keeping things in shared memory. On Hopper you have new features like the Tensor Memory Accelerator and warpgroup matrix multiplies, and asynchrony becomes central: you want data movement and compute overlapping, so the kernel looks quite different. Blackwell changes things again. If you just port the old kernel, you might leave half the performance on the table.

On the other hand, nobody wants to rewrite everything from scratch every two years, and now there's real diversity: AMD, the various accelerator startups, the TPUs. So the way I think about it is in terms of layers of abstraction. The ideas are pretty portable. Things like IO-awareness, thinking about the memory hierarchy, tiling, and fusing operations to avoid round trips to slow memory apply to basically every chip. The algorithms transfer well; it's the implementation details that don't.

So what we've tried to do is build better abstractions at the right level. Something like CUTLASS and CuTe gives you composable building blocks for layouts and tiles, and more recently we've been pushing on Python-level DSLs so you can express a kernel at a higher level and still get close to hand-tuned performance. Triton is another good example of that philosophy. You give up maybe a little bit at the very top end, but you gain a lot in productivity and portability.

I also think the hardware and the models are going to co-evolve. Architectures that map well onto whatever the hardware is good at, mostly big matrix multiplies, tend to win. So part of portability is designing algorithms that lean on the primitives every vendor is going to make fast anyway. If your model is mostly matmuls with a bit of cleverness around memory movement, you're in good shape no matter what chip comes next.

And honestly, AI itself is starting to help here. Using models to help write and tune kernels for new hardware could shrink that porting cost a lot over the next few years. I'm pretty optimistic about that.

r001.rationale: It says peak performance requires hardware-specific code and illustrates that with newer generation-specific features such as Hopper’s Tensor Memory Accelerator and warpgroup matrix multiplies.

r002.rationale: It says FlashAttention has had to be rethought with each generation, that Hopper’s kernel looks quite different, and that an old kernel may leave substantial performance unused.

r003.rationale: It describes abstractions as useful for portability across different chips, but does not clearly state that they help move between successive Nvidia generations from the same manufacturer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because honestly a big part of the pain of working on FlashAttention has been exactly this. We wrote FlashAttention 1 for Ampere, and then Hopper came out and the hardware changed enough that a lot of the tricks just didn't carry over. You get things like TMA for asynchronous memory copies, warpgroup-level matrix multiply instructions, a different register and shared memory story, and suddenly the kernel you wrote carefully for A100 is leaving a lot of performance on the table on H100. So we basically had to rewrite it. And then Blackwell comes along and you're looking at tensor memory and a different programming model again.

So the first thing I'd say is that portability is kind of in tension with peak performance, and I don't think that tension fully goes away. The reason the hardware changes is that the vendors are finding new ways to move data more efficiently, and if you want to be at the frontier you have to use those features. The abstraction that hides them from you is, almost by definition, going to cost you something.

But I don't think the answer is "everyone rewrites everything every two years." The way I think about it is in layers. At the bottom you have a small number of kernels that really matter, attention, matmul, maybe a few others, and for those it's worth having experts hand-tune per architecture. That's a finite amount of work, and it's where most of the FLOPs go anyway. Then above that you want a layer like Triton, or some of these newer DSLs, where a researcher can write something reasonably fast without knowing what a wgmma instruction is, and the compiler takes on more of the burden of mapping to the hardware. That layer is where portability should live, and the compiler folks are the ones absorbing the hardware churn so that everyone else doesn't have to.

The other thing I'd point out is that even though the instructions change, the principles don't change much. It's still about the memory hierarchy. It's still about asynchrony, overlapping data movement with compute. It's still about keeping the tensor cores fed. If you understand those ideas, then moving to a new architecture is more like learning a new dialect than a new language. The specific primitives are different, but you know what you're looking for. So when I teach people about this, I try to emphasize those ideas rather than any particular API.

And then the last piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that the model side has some say here too. Architectures that are friendlier to hardware, that have fewer weird operations, more things that look like large matmuls, are inherently more portable because the hardware vendors optimize matmul first on every chip. Part of why I've been interested in things like Mamba and state space models is that question of co-design, what does a model look like if you think about the hardware from the beginning. If we're a bit disciplined about that, then portability gets easier not just across NVIDIA generations but across AMD, TPUs, whatever comes next.

r001.rationale: The response describes new hardware features and says vendors use them to move data more efficiently, but does not clearly present increasingly specialized components as the main way to gain further GPU performance.

r002.rationale: It says FlashAttention 1 was written for Ampere, Hopper changed the hardware enough that many tricks no longer carried over, and they had to rewrite it.

r003.rationale: It recommends a portability layer such as Triton to absorb hardware churn, in a discussion of successive NVIDIA generations from Ampere through Hopper to Blackwell.

astra-6.text:
I think about portability at two levels. One is correctness: can the same code run on a new GPU? The other, which is much harder, is performance: does that code actually use the new GPU well?

For something like attention, the underlying idea—reducing data movement by doing more work on chip—can carry across architectures. But the best implementation depends on the hardware: how much shared memory you have, how fast matrix multiplication is relative to memory access, and what mechanisms exist for moving data asynchronously. Those details can change how you partition and schedule the computation.

So I wouldn’t expect one low-level kernel to stay optimal forever. What I’d like is to preserve the algorithm and express enough of its structure that a compiler or a relatively small hardware-specific layer can adapt it. The challenge is finding that boundary: how much can you abstract away while still giving developers control over the things that matter for performance?

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting implementations to hardware differences, but does not present increasingly specialized hardware components as the main source of further GPU performance gains.

r002.rationale: It says low-level kernels may stop being optimal, but does not state that successive Nvidia GPU generations require substantial software rewrites.

r003.rationale: It favors abstractions that preserve algorithms across architectures, but does not specify portability between successive generations from the same manufacturer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about portability at two levels: can the code run on a new architecture, and can it run efficiently? The second one is much harder. You can write something that’s mathematically identical across GPUs, but the best way to divide the work, move data, and overlap computation with memory access can change quite a bit.

For attention, the high-level idea of reducing memory traffic carries over. But you still have to adapt how you implement it to the hardware. A new architecture might have different mechanisms for asynchronous data movement, or a different balance between compute throughput and memory bandwidth. Those details affect which algorithmic choices work well.

So I wouldn’t expect one handwritten kernel to remain optimal forever. What I’d like is a programming model where we can preserve the core algorithm and express the scheduling choices separately, so adapting to a new GPU doesn’t mean rewriting everything. The challenge is finding abstractions that make that easier while still giving you enough control to get close to the hardware’s performance limits.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on adapting algorithms, scheduling, and programming abstractions; it does not present increasingly specialized hardware components as the main source of further GPU performance gains.

r002.rationale: It says adaptation to a new GPU should not require rewriting everything and does not state that successive Nvidia generations require substantial software rewrites.

r003.rationale: It values abstractions for adapting to a new GPU, but does not identify movement between successive generations from the same manufacturer.
